The motif is a bat. In Chinese, the pronunciation of “蝠” (fú) is associated with “福” (fú), meaning good fortune. For this reason, bats have long been cherished as a highly auspicious motif symbolizing “bringing good fortune,” good fortune and longevity. The smooth curves of the large outstretched wings and the bat’s distinctive expression are intricately and delicately carved in three dimensions. 【 Condition 】 This item is a pre-owned product. At that time, traditional Japanese clothing such as kimono had no pockets, so small items like coin purses or medicine containers were carried by hanging them from cords tied to the sash (帯obi). To prevent these items from slipping through, netsuke were used as toggles to secure the cord above the sash. To prevent these items from slipping through, netsuke were used as toggles to secure the cord above the sash. title: Antique Japanese Netsuke Skull Snake Signed Boxwood Edo Period Carving Rare
description: Thank you for viewing this piece and taking the time to consider it. This is an original antique Japanese netsuke hand carved from boxwood depicting a skull with a snake wrapped around it. The carving shows strong detail in the skull features and the carefully carved scales of the snake, along with the warm natural patina that develops over time on authentic handmade boxwood netsuke. Subjects such as skulls and serpents appear in Japanese art as symbolic reminders of mortality, transformation, and the cycle of life. The compact form and expressive carving make this an especially striking example of traditional netsuke craftsmanship. Netsuke were historically worn with kimono as functional miniature sculptures used to secure personal items such as inrō or tobacco pouches. Today they are highly valued by collectors as small works of art representing the craftsmanship and culture of the Edo and early Meiji periods. This Koi Fish one is really good looking. I am not selling it with a wooden display platform, because it actually looks better without it. I've used google image search on it like 20 times and I can't find another one made of a tagua nut, but I'm positive that's what this is. The carving and painting on this are both pretty remarkable. The Tagua nuts were harvested in Zambia (Africa) and then sent to China for carving. The Tagua tree is a palm tree that grows freely in some subtropical climates, but is absolutely not grown in China. The Tagua nut is very hard and takes on a beautiful ivory or darker than ivory, amber color. For this reason, Tagua is sometimes known as Vegetable Ivory. The composition of the Tagua nut is so similar to mammal tusk that it is difficult for some people to tell them apart. For me, I feel like I can easily tell them apart. The carved tagua nuts I'm selling here are wonderful, but I don't think they look like they are creme-color, or light enough to be mistaken for ivory. Perhaps they have turned to amber over time? description: Hand Carved and Painted TAGUA NUT BABY IN A NUT from Hong Kong Rare Vintage Grown in Zambia/Zaire, Sent to China where they're carved, Sold in Hong Kong at Jade Market which is a huge seller of all kinds of items you can't get anywhere else. THIS ONE IS LIKE A BABY WRAPPED UP IN A TAGUA NUT. So, in this case, you can see what a tagua nut looks like, because the baby is carved into the side of it, and the rest of it remains. I assume it's polished up pretty well. (It does not come with the wooden display stand.) The Tagua nuts were harvested in Zambia (Africa) and then sent to China for carving. The Tagua tree is a palm tree that grows freely in some subtropical climates, but is absolutely not grown in China. The Tagua nut is very hard and takes on a beautiful ivory or darker than ivory, amber color. For this reason, Tagua is sometimes known as Vegetable Ivory. The composition of the Tagua nut is so similar to mammal tusk that it is difficult for some people to tell them apart. For me, I feel like I can easily tell them apart. The carved tagua nuts I'm selling here are wonderful, but I don't think they look like they are creme-color, or light enough to be mistaken for ivory. Perhaps they have turned to amber over time? title: Antique Japanese Netsuke - Man with Turtle On Back, Porcelain, Signed
description: Antique Japanese Netsuke: Man with Turtle on his Back, Signed Porcelain A charming porcelain netsuke depicting a cheerful, rotund figure with a large turtle on his back. The man is modeled with expressive facial features and wears traditional robes decorated with detailed polychrome enameling. The turtle is rendered with a finely painted shell and naturalistic features. The surface has the smooth, glossy finish typical of porcelain netsuke, with bright overglaze enamel decoration applied by hand. The underside bears a small painted signature or artist’s mark in black ink; the characters are stylized and partially worn, consistent with workshop‑level signatures found on late‑Meiji to early‑Shōwa porcelain netsuke. Two himotoshi openings are drilled through the base for suspension. Porcelain netsuke represent a distinct tradition from carved material examples and were popular for their whimsical subjects and colorful decoration. The theme of a man carrying a turtle is an auspicious one in Japanese art, symbolizing longevity, perseverance, and good fortune. The quality of the modeling and enameling suggests skilled workshop production from the early 20th century.

description: Hand Carved and Painted TAGUA NUT MERMAID from Hong Kong Rare Vintage Fabulous Grown in Zambia/Zaire, Sent to China where they're carved, Sold in Hong Kong at Jade Market which is a huge seller of all kinds of items you can't get anywhere else. Like all mermaids, she is fabulous. She is half naked, like a real mermaid. She comes with a small wooden display base, and is signed where her knee would be if she had knees. It is kind of painted red, so you can't miss it. This is a nicely carved nut. She is a good-looking mermaid. I like how her hair goes. The Tagua nuts were harvested in Zambia (Africa) and then sent to China for carving. The Tagua tree is a palm tree that grows freely in some subtropical climates, but is absolutely not grown in China. The Tagua nut is very hard and takes on a beautiful ivory or darker than ivory, amber color. For this reason, Tagua is sometimes known as Vegetable Ivory. The composition of the Tagua nut is so similar to mammal tusk that it is difficult for some people to tell them apart. For me, I feel like I can easily tell them apart. The carved tagua nuts I'm selling here are wonderful, but I don't think they look like they are creme-color, or light enough to be mistaken for ivory. Perhaps they have turned to amber over time? description: This piece comes from a private collection I inherited from my grandmother, who was a dedicated antique dealer and collector with a deep appreciation for traditional Japanese art. This item is a Japanese netsuke, a finely carved miniature sculpture traditionally used as a toggle to secure small containers (such as an inrō) to the sash (obi) of a kimono. The carving depicts two monkeys (saru) in a dynamic, intertwined composition, skillfully wrapped around a central form. The interaction between the figures reflects a classic theme in Japanese art, where monkeys are used to mirror human behavior, symbolizing social hierarchy, connection, and playful expression. The sculptor captures a sense of movement and emotion, giving the piece a lifelike presence in hand. The surface shows a rich, warm patina consistent with age, adding depth and character that only time can create. The compact, well-balanced form and expressive detailing are qualities that make netsuke highly sought after by collectors. The underside bears a carved signature that appears to read Kogyoku ( 光玉 ), further enhancing its appeal. This specific set is unique in that it is crafted entirely from natural bovine bone, including the scabbard and the decorative blade. It serves as a beautiful representation of Chinese folk art and scholarly desk objects. Material & Artistry: • Scabbard: Hand-carved from natural bovine (cow) bone, featuring an intricate, continuous scene of a traditional Chinese dragon among clouds. The detail is crisp and wraps around the entire housing. • Blade & Handle: The utility knife is also crafted from natural bovine bone. The handle features incised auspicious symbols, including the bat (happiness) and "Shou" longevity characters. • Chopsticks: Two hand-shaped wood chopsticks are included and fit perfectly into the scabbard's side slots. Condition: Excellent vintage condition. The bovine bone has developed a rich, creamy patina over the decades. All carvings are sharp, and the brass retaining bands are tight and secure. No cracks or significant chips to the bone elements. Specifications: • Era: Circa 1930s–1940s • Origin: China • Materials: Bovine Bone (Bos taurus), Wood, Brass. Why this is a premium set: • All-Bone Construction: The inclusion of a carved bone scabbard and blade makes this significantly rarer than common wood-and-steel sets. • Dragon Motif: The high-relief dragon carving on the scabbard elevates this from a tool to a piece of fine decorative art. • Gift Potential:
